title: 6 Best Deck Sealers in 2026: Clear Finishes Ranked by Upkeep
metaDescription: TWP 1500 is the best deck sealer for most wood decks: it soaks in, fades evenly and recoats without stripping. 6 clear and natural-tone picks compared.
keywords: best product for sealing a wood deck
what is the best waterproofing for an older deck
intro:
The best deck sealer for most wood decks is TWP 1500, an oil-based penetrating finish that soaks in, fades evenly and recoats with a cleaning instead of a stripper. Ready Seal's lightest tint is the easiest to apply without lap marks, and DEFY Extreme Clear is the water-based choice for low-VOC states.

A clear deck sealer keeps water out and leaves the grain alone, but it does very little about sun. No clear lasts five years on a sunny deck, so the real question is which one goes on cleanly, beads water longest in your climate and is easy enough to recoat that you will actually do it. That is how the six picks below are ranked.
quickAnswer: Buy TWP 1500 or Ready Seal Natural Cedar for most decks; both penetrate, fade gracefully and never need stripping between coats. Choose DEFY Extreme Clear if you need a water-based product, Seal-Once Marine near water, and Thompson's WaterSeal if you accept yearly recoats on a budget. Expect one to two years from a clear on a sunny deck.

sections.body:

| TWP 1500 Series | Most cedar and pressure-treated decks | Oil-based penetrating preservative |
| Ready Seal Natural Cedar | First-timers, big decks, even color | Oil-based, no back-brushing per maker |
| DEFY Extreme Clear | Low-VOC states, short weather windows | Water-based with zinc oxide |
| Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced | Tight budgets, yearly recoats | Clear water repellent |
| Olympic Maximum Clear | Local Lowe's shoppers | Water-based clear sealant |
| Seal-Once Marine | Decks by ponds, lakes and pools | Water-based penetrating, lower solvent |

Clear sealer protects against water; pigment protects against sun. If you want grain-perfect color and accept yearly upkeep, buy a sealer. If you want two or three years between projects, buy something with color, which is what our [best deck stain rankings](/best-deck-stain-reviews/) cover.

Lightly tinted sealers such as Ready Seal Natural Cedar sit in the middle and are the best compromise for most owners who want a natural-looking deck.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Deck Sealers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The ranking draws on manufacturer data sheets, label coverage and recoat guidance, VOC and availability limits, and recurring patterns in owner reports on how each product ages on real decks. No weathering trials were run for this guide. Each pick is matched to the deck and owner it fits best.

### Best Overall: TWP 1500 Series Wood Preservative

TWP, short for Total Wood Preservative, is a long-running oil-based line that deck restoration contractors often use on cedar and pressure-treated decks. The 1500 Series soaks into the boards instead of building a coating, so when it wears it looks drier and lighter rather than flaking off in patches.

That failure mode is why it ranks first. Maintenance is a cleaning and a fresh coat, with no stripping between cycles. The line includes a clear and several lightly toned versions; the toned ones carry more pigment and generally hold up longer in sun. The label describes water and mildew resistance, and the brand positions it as a preservative rather than a cosmetic finish. Expect the wood to warm a shade even in the clearest version. The drawbacks are practical. Some formulas are restricted in low-VOC states, it is harder to buy in person than big-box brands, and it needs warm, dry days to cure. Five-gallon pails lower the cost per gallon on bigger decks.

**Pros:** penetrating oil with no surface film; labeled as a preservative with mildew resistance; clear and lightly toned options; recoats after cleaning only; long track record with deck contractors.

**Cons:** not sold in every state because of VOC rules; usually ordered online or from dealers; slower dry time than water-based sealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=TWP+1500+Series+wood+preservative&tag=sktiger-20)

### Easiest to Apply: Ready Seal Exterior Wood Stain and Sealer, Natural Cedar

Ready Seal's reputation rests on being hard to mess up. The maker says it needs no back-brushing and leaves no lap marks, and owner feedback largely agrees: people who fought streaky finishes on earlier decks often report that Ready Seal was the first product that came out even.

It is an oil-based penetrating finish that goes on with a pump sprayer, roller or brush, which speeds up big decks and long railings. Natural Cedar is about the lightest shade in the line, so it reads as a warm, nearly clear finish rather than a stain. That small dose of pigment is useful, because it blocks more UV than a true clear and slows graying. Two things catch first-time users. The color looks light while wet and deepens over roughly two weeks as it cures, so judge the result after that. And it needs warm, dry weather plus mineral spirits for cleanup. It is not a true clear, but for most decks it is the better long-term choice.

**Pros:** marketed as no back-brushing and no lap marks; spray, roll or brush; light tint adds UV protection while grain shows; forgiving for first-timers; sold in one- and five-gallon sizes.

**Cons:** color develops over about two weeks; oil-based cleanup and longer dry time; not a true clear.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ready+Seal+Natural+Cedar+stain+and+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Water-Based Clear: DEFY Extreme Clear Wood Sealer

DEFY Extreme Clear is a water-based penetrating sealer that tries to narrow the gap between clear finishes and real sun protection. It uses zinc oxide nanoparticles, which scatter UV without adding the visible color that pigment would.

That does not turn it into a semi-transparent stain, but it gives a clear a better shot at holding natural color than older wax-based repellents. Because it is water-based, cleanup is soap and water, odor is mild and it can ship to states with strict VOC limits. It also dries fast, which helps when the forecast gives you a single good afternoon. The tradeoffs are typical of water-based finishes. Apply it on a day that stays warm and dry into the evening, because dew or a shower before it sets can leave it blotchy. Owners also note it looks flatter than an oil, without the warm, wet look oil gives cedar. Expect yearly recoats on a sunny deck and longer gaps in shade.

**Pros:** soap-and-water cleanup and low odor; zinc oxide for better UV resistance than typical clears; fast drying; sold in low-VOC states; penetrates rather than building a heavy film.

**Cons:** needs warm, dry conditions with no dew while drying; looks flatter than oil; shorter life on sun-baked floors.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEFY+Extreme+Clear+wood+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: Thompson's WaterSeal Advanced Natural Wood Protector

Thompson's WaterSeal is the deck sealer most people have heard of, and the Advanced Natural Wood Protector is the brand's current mainstream clear. Its strength is reach: nearly every hardware store carries it, it costs less than most competitors and water beads on it impressively the day it goes on.

For a deck you plan to stain with color later, a fence or a shed, that is often enough. Where it falls short is life on open horizontal boards. With no pigment and limited UV defense, the wood keeps graying, and the beading on high-traffic boards typically fades within a year. Plenty of owners accept that and simply recoat each spring. The usual complaint, a sticky or shiny surface, nearly always comes from putting a second coat over a first that is still repelling water. Do a water drop test before each recoat and apply only where the wood absorbs. On that understanding, it is a fair low-cost deck water seal.

**Pros:** sold almost everywhere; low price per gallon; easy pump sprayer or roller application; strong immediate beading.

**Cons:** very little UV protection so wood still grays; plan on yearly recoats on decks; coats stacked too soon turn tacky.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Thompson%27s+WaterSeal+Advanced+Natural+Wood+Protector&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Big-Box Clear: Olympic Maximum Waterproofing Sealant, Clear

Olympic Maximum is the flagship deck finish family at Lowe's, and the clear waterproofing sealant is its no-color member. It is water-based, so it cleans up with soap and water, which suits owners who would rather skip solvent.

The label calls out water repellency and mildew resistance on the coating, and the wider Maximum line includes toned, semi-transparent and solid versions. That range makes it easy to step up to more color and UV protection later without changing systems, which is handy if you shop locally. Like every clear here, it does not stop sun from graying the wood. It also behaves a little more like a coating than a pure penetrating oil, so many years of heavy layering can leave a surface that eventually needs a stripper instead of a cleaner. Apply thin coats, back-brush and recoat only when the water test shows absorption. As a step up from basic repellents that you can buy today, it is a solid option.

**Pros:** widely stocked at Lowe's; water-based with easy cleanup; mildew-resistant coating per the label; tinted versions in the same line; reasonable price.

**Cons:** clear version still lets wood gray; can build a light film with repeated coats; needs careful prep.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Olympic+Maximum+waterproofing+sealant+clear&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Near Water: Seal-Once Marine Premium Wood Sealer

Seal-Once Marine is a water-based penetrating sealer sold for docks, piers and wood that sits near water, so it is a sensible pick for a deck beside a pond, lake or pool. It soaks in rather than forming a thick film, and the brand emphasizes lower solvent content than traditional oil sealers.

That matters when runoff or overspray will reach water or plantings you care about. Owners generally describe it as easy to spray or roll, quick to dry and easy to clean up. The clear version shares the limits of every clear: it keeps water out but does little to stop sun graying the surface, so choose a tinted version if UV defense is the goal. It costs more than basic repellents and is more often bought online or from marine suppliers than at a home center. If your deck sits in open sun far from any water, a toned oil may be the better value. Near the shoreline or a pool, start here.

**Pros:** water-based penetrating polymer; marketed for docks and marine wood; low odor and easy cleanup; clear and tinted versions; no thick film.

**Cons:** harder to find in stores; higher price than basic repellents; clear version offers limited UV defense.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Seal-Once+Marine+premium+wood+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Deck Sealer or Deck Stain: Which Do You Need?
sections.body:
Choose a clear sealer when the wood is new or freshly cleaned, you like its natural color and you will recoat often. Choose a stain when the deck sits in full afternoon sun or you want longer gaps between projects.

### What the labels mean

Sealer, sealant, water repellent and stain get used interchangeably on store shelves. In this guide, a deck sealer is a clear or very lightly tinted finish whose main job is keeping liquid water out. A stain carries enough pigment to change color and block a real share of sunlight. Many cans say stain and sealer in one, and those sit on a sliding scale between the two.

### When a sealer is the right call

Cedar, redwood and tropical hardwood are the usual candidates, because their color is why people bought them. A clear coat stops them soaking up rain, swelling and cupping while the grain shows exactly as it is.

### When to skip both

If boards are badly weathered, split or covered in peeling film, a clear will hide nothing and a penetrating product cannot get through the old coating. Those decks need stripping to bare wood or a different approach, such as the solid stains and resurfacers in our [deck paint guide](/best-deck-paint/).

sections.heading: How Do Clear Deck Sealers Work?
sections.body:
Clear deck sealers fall into three chemistry families, and the family predicts how long the finish lasts and how it fails.

### Wax-based water repellents

The oldest type is a thin carrier loaded with paraffin wax that lodges in surface pores and makes water bead. It is cheap and quick but sits near the surface and wears off fast under feet and sun.

### Penetrating oils

Drying oils such as linseed or soy, often with paraffinic oils, are thinned to soak into the top fraction of an inch and harden inside the wood. There is no film to peel; they fade and dry out instead, so the next coat is clean and reapply. They usually warm the wood a shade even when labeled clear.

### Water-based penetrating sealers

Acrylic or other polymer resins small enough to enter the wood. They clean up with soap and water, carry far less solvent and usually dry to the touch in an hour or two. Some add zinc oxide or transparent iron oxide for UV help without visible color.

| Type | Typical life on a sunny deck | Cleanup | Main tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wax-based repellent | About 1 year | Varies | Cheapest, shortest life |
| Penetrating oil | 1 to 2 years | Mineral spirits | Darkens wood, slower dry |
| Water-based penetrating | 1 to 2 years | Soap and water | Flatter look, needs warm dry weather |
| Lightly tinted versions | 2 to 3 years | Same as base | Slight color shift |

None of these, in clear form, stops UV from breaking down lignin, the natural glue in the wood surface. That is why a clear deck still grays.

sections.heading: What to Compare on a Deck Sealer Label
sections.body:
Check five things before you buy: penetration, mildewcide, the application window, VOC availability and the recoat method.

### Penetrating vs film-forming

On a floor, a penetrating product almost always beats a film. Deck boards flex, swell with moisture and take abrasion from shoes, chairs and grills. A film cracks along those stresses and lets water in behind it. A penetrating finish has nothing to crack, so wear shows as gradual fading.

### Mildewcide

Shaded decks and humid climates grow mildew on almost any finish, and oils give it food. Look for a label that lists a mildewcide or calls the product a wood preservative, especially for a deck under trees in a humid state.

### Application window

Labels list a temperature range, often from about 40 or 50 degrees into the low 90s, and a rain-free period afterward. Water-based products want warmer, drier conditions; oils tolerate cooler days but stay tacky longer. A product you cannot apply in your usual season is the wrong product.

### VOC limits

Several states and air districts cap solvent content. Some oil sealers are reformulated or not shipped to those areas, so check the maker's state list first if you live in California, the Northeast or the Mid-Atlantic.

### Recoat method

The best deck sealer for a homeowner is one that recoats without stripping. Most penetrating products need only a cleaning. A few water-based clears build a light film over several coats and eventually need sanding or stripping.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Sealer for Your Type of Decking?
sections.body:
Match the sealer to the species: lightly tinted oils for pine and cedar, toned finishes for redwood, hardwood formulas for ipe, and nothing at all for composite.

### Pressure-treated pine

This is most American decking, and it gains least from a true clear because its color is not the attraction. Treated pine arrives wet and will not take any finish until it dries; wait until water drops soak in within a few minutes. Once dry, a lightly tinted penetrating oil or water-based sealer is a better value than a pure clear.

### Cedar

Soft, absorbent and rich in natural oils, cedar suits penetrating oils, and toned clears with a hint of cedar color hold the look longer. Avoid aggressive pressure washing, which erodes the soft earlywood and leaves a fuzzy surface that soaks up finish unevenly.

### Redwood

Redwood behaves like cedar with more tannin and a color that bleaches fast in sun. A clear keeps it dry but rarely keeps it red; a redwood-toned penetrating finish is the realistic answer.

### Tropical hardwoods

Ipe, cumaru and garapa are so dense that many sealers sit on top and turn sticky. Use a hardwood formula, apply thin and wipe off every drop of excess, or let the boards weather to silver and clean them once a year. The hardwood oils in our [exterior wood sealer guide](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) are made for this.

### Composite and PVC

Do not seal composite or PVC boards. They are not designed to absorb a sealer, and most makers advise against coatings. Clean them with a product the board maker approves.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Way to Seal an Older Deck?
sections.body:
On an older deck, the cleaning matters more than the can. Clean, brighten, dry, then apply a penetrating sealer in thin, even coats.

### Clean and brighten

Use a sodium percarbonate or other oxygen-based deck cleaner to lift gray fibers, dirt and mildew, then an oxalic acid brightener to neutralize the cleaner and bring back the wood's color. Skip chlorine bleach, which damages fibers and leaves blotches.

### Pressure wash gently

Keep pressure low, use a wide fan tip, hold the wand a foot or more away and move with the grain. A rotary [surface cleaner for a pressure washer](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) keeps the spray even on wide areas if it runs at reduced pressure.

### Remove failing film

Clear penetrating sealers cannot bond through peeling paint or solid stain. Use a deck stripper, then brightener. On small areas, sand with 60 to 80 grit; finer grits close the surface too much.

### Let it dry

Most labels ask for 24 to 48 hours of dry weather. A pin moisture meter reading in the low to mid teens is generally ready. Without a meter, sprinkle water: if it soaks in within a few minutes, the wood will take finish.

### Fix the hidden parts

Treat field cuts on pressure-treated lumber with an end-cut preservative, check that hardware is hot-dip galvanized or stainless, and look at ledger and joist tops, which stay wet longest. Sealer on the top boards does nothing for framing that never dries.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply Deck Sealer Without Lap Marks or Sticky Spots?
sections.body:
Work in shade, coat a few boards at a time along their full length, back-brush everything and never flood the surface.

### Step by step

1. **Pick the right day.** Early morning after the dew dries, or late afternoon on the shaded side, with at least a full day of dry weather ahead.
2. **Railings first.** Do vertical parts first, then the floor, working toward the exit. Stairs come last.
3. **Two or three boards at a time.** Run each group the full length of the board so wet finish never meets dried finish mid-board.
4. **Back-brush.** Follow a pump sprayer or roller with a brush or pad to push sealer into the grain and spread puddles. This one habit improves both looks and life.
5. **Wipe the excess.** Anything the wood cannot absorb dries tacky. On dense or new wood, wipe up pooled sealer after the label's wait, often 15 to 30 minutes. Follow the label on one coat versus a second coat wet on wet.

### How much to buy

Labels typically list 150 to 300 square feet per gallon on smooth wood and as little as 100 to 150 on rough or weathered boards. Railings with pickets often add 40 to 60 percent to the floor area, and stairs add treads, risers and stringers. A 300 square foot deck with rails and stairs usually needs two to three gallons for a first coat.

### Oily rags

Rags soaked in drying oils can heat as they cure and catch fire. Spread them flat outdoors to dry, or keep them under water in a closed metal can until disposal.

sections.heading: How Long Does Deck Sealer Last, and When Should You Recoat?
sections.body:
On an open, sunny deck, most clear sealers keep beading water for one to two years on the floor and somewhat longer on railings. Lightly tinted versions typically last two to three years.

### The water drop test

Sprinkle water on the boards that get the most sun and traffic. If it beads, the sealer is working. If it darkens the wood and soaks in within about a minute, it is time to clean and recoat. Check in late spring and again in early fall.

### Where it fails first

The path from the door to the grill, the steps and boards in front of a south-facing railing go first. Shaded sections may still repel water years later. Most penetrating oils blend, so you can recoat only the worn areas; water-based products usually look best when the whole floor is redone.

### Do not stack coats

Fresh sealer cannot soak into wood that still repels water, so it sits on top and turns sticky. That is the most common complaint about clear products, and it is a timing problem, not a defect.

### A practical rhythm

Plan on a fresh coat every 12 to 24 months on floors and every two to three years on railings. Each recoat needs lighter prep than the first: cleaner, rinse, brightener if the wood darkened and a day or two of drying. If that pace feels like too much, move to a semi-transparent stain. Compare cost per year of protection rather than price per can, because a cheap clear that needs yearly work can cost more over time than a tinted product that lasts three times as long.

mistakes.title: Sealing new pressure-treated boards right away
mistakes.body: Fresh treated lumber is saturated from the treatment process, so sealer applied over it cannot soak in. It sits on top, turns tacky or fails within months. Wait until water dropped on the boards absorbs within a few minutes, which can take weeks or months depending on climate.

mistakes.title: Expecting a clear sealer to stop graying
mistakes.body: Clear sealers are water repellents first. With no pigment, UV still breaks down the surface and cedar and redwood drift toward gray. If keeping color is the priority, choose a lightly tinted or semi-transparent product and accept a slight color shift for far better sun protection.

mistakes.title: Blasting the deck with high pressure
mistakes.body: A narrow tip held close gouges soft wood, raises the grain and leaves a fuzzy surface that absorbs sealer unevenly. Let a deck cleaner do the chemical work, keep pressure low, hold the wand back and follow the grain. On cedar, a garden hose and scrub brush is often enough.

mistakes.title: Recoating while the old coat still beads water
mistakes.body: New sealer over a finish that still repels water stays on the surface, dries sticky and collects dirt. Always do a water drop test first, recoat only the boards that absorb, and wipe off anything the wood has not taken in within the label's wait time.

mistakes.title: Leaving railings and stairs out of the estimate
mistakes.body: Pickets, rails, treads, risers and stringers can add half again to the floor area. Running out mid-project forces a stop in the middle of a section and leaves lap lines. Measure every surface, use the rough-wood coverage figure for older boards and buy an extra gallon.

faqs.q: What is the best deck sealer?
faqs.a: TWP 1500 is the best deck sealer for most wood decks because it penetrates, fades evenly and recoats without stripping. Ready Seal Natural Cedar is the easiest to apply evenly, DEFY Extreme Clear is the top water-based choice, Seal-Once Marine suits decks near water, and Thompson's WaterSeal is the budget option if you accept yearly recoats.

faqs.q: What is the highest rated deck sealer for natural color?
faqs.a: For a deck that keeps a natural look, owners rate lightly tinted penetrating sealers such as Ready Seal Natural Cedar and the lighter TWP 1500 tones highest, because a small amount of pigment slows graying far better than a true clear. If you need a true clear, DEFY Extreme Clear adds zinc oxide for more UV resistance than basic repellents.

faqs.q: How long does a clear deck sealer last?
faqs.a: On an open, sunny deck, most clear sealers keep beading water for about one to two years on the floor boards and a bit longer on railings. Shade, climate and foot traffic shift that a lot, and lightly tinted versions usually last two to three years. Use a water drop test to decide when to recoat.

faqs.q: What is the best waterproofing for an older deck?
faqs.a: For an older wood deck that is still sound, the best waterproofing is a thorough clean and brighten followed by a penetrating oil sealer such as TWP 1500 or Ready Seal. If old film is peeling, strip it first. If boards are split, checked or mismatched, a solid stain or resurfacer usually works better than a clear sealer.

faqs.q: Is oil-based or water-based deck sealer better?
faqs.a: Neither wins outright. Oil-based sealers soak deeper, warm the color and fade gradually, which makes recoating easy. Water-based sealers dry faster, clean up with soap and water, smell less and are legal in low-VOC states. Choose oil for weathered wood in moderate weather and water-based for short weather windows or strict VOC rules.

faqs.q: Can you put deck sealer over an old stain?
faqs.a: You can put a penetrating sealer over an old penetrating stain once it has worn enough that water soaks in, after cleaning the deck. You cannot put a penetrating sealer over solid stain, paint or peeling film, because it has nothing to soak into. Strip those finishes first or choose a product designed to go over them.

faqs.q: Do composite decks need deck sealer?
faqs.a: No. Composite and PVC decking are not designed to absorb a wood sealer, and most makers advise against coating the boards. A sealer can leave a slippery or blotchy film and may affect the warranty. Clean composite with a cleaner the board maker approves, and treat any wood framing, stringers or fascia separately.

bottomLine: For most decks, TWP 1500 or Ready Seal's lightest tint is the deck sealer to buy: both soak in, fade evenly and recoat with a cleaning instead of a stripper. DEFY Extreme Clear is the water-based answer for low-VOC states and short weather windows, Seal-Once Marine fits decks beside water, and Thompson's is a fair budget repellent if yearly recoats do not bother you. The deck will only look as good as the prep and timing allow, so clean and brighten, let the wood dry, back-brush every section and recoat when water stops beading. If you want more than two years between projects, step up to a pigmented stain.
